desc:
The string expr is an arithmetic expression in one variable x, without spaces. It is built from the variable x, non-negative integer literals, the binary operators +, -, * and round brackets. Priorities are the usual ones (* before + and -, equal priorities left to right). A minus sign may also be used as a unary operator, but only at the very start of the expression or directly after an opening bracket (for example -x*x+3 or 2*(-x+3)); it negates the single term that follows it.

Multiplying out all brackets turns the expression into a polynomial c0 + c1x + c2x2 + .... Return its coefficients as an array [c0, c1, ...], each reduced modulo 1,000,000,007 to the range 0..1,000,000,006 (so -1 becomes 1000000006). Drop zero coefficients at the high end; the zero polynomial is returned as [0].

Examples: (x+1)*(x+1) gives [1, 2, 1]. (x-1)*(x+1) gives [1000000006, 0, 1] (that is x2 - 1). x-x gives [0].
constraints: expr contains only x, digits, + - *, ( and ) and is valid as described; literals are in [0, 10<sup>9</sup>] without leading zeros (except "0")
Brackets can be nested up to 500 levels deep
The answer has at most 1,000 coefficients
hints: Represent every sub-expression by the list of its coefficients, so that an expression is just a value of a new kind. Addition and subtraction are element-wise, multiplication is a convolution.
Evaluate the expression like an ordinary calculator, with a stack of values (polynomials) and a stack of operators, but let the 'numbers' be coefficient lists: x is [0, 1] and the literal 5 is [5].

Treat a unary minus as 0 - term: when a - appears at the start or right after (, push the value [0] first. Reduce all coefficients modulo 109+7 after each operation and strip high-end zeros only at the very end.
editorial: The expression grammar does not care what the values are, only that +, - and * exist on them. Polynomials form a ring, so the usual shunting-yard evaluation works if each operand is a coefficient list: the variable x is [0, 1], a literal k is [k mod p].

Addition and subtraction combine the lists position by position (padding the shorter one with zeros). Multiplication convolves: res[i + j] += a[i] * b[j]. A unary minus is handled by pushing the constant polynomial [0] before the minus, so it becomes the binary 0 - term with the correct priority (-x*x is 0 - (x*x)). The stacks make the evaluation iterative, so nesting depth is no problem.

The cost of a multiplication is the product of the two lengths. Since the lengths of the operands add up to at most the number of x in the expression, all the multiplications together cost at most O(m2) where m is the number of x characters (at most about 1,000 here); additions cost O(length) each. Skipping zero coefficients in the inner loop makes sparse cases even faster.
